results.summary: This design is a 40-bit shift register that compares the shifted value against a hardcoded 40-bit number and drives its output high only on a match. It is used by shifting bits in via the data and clock inputs, with each rising clock edge advancing the register. Testing with the known number requires only a DIP switch for data, a button for clock, and an LED on the output; without the number, reverse engineering or side-channel attacks are suggested. The project is notable as a hardware puzzle challenge rather than a functional block, and its documentation is sufficient to describe the intended use.

This design inverts every input line using eight inverters, with the inverted signals driving the seven segment outputs and one additional output. It is tested by toggling input switches and observing that the corresponding LEDs turn off when the input is on. No external hardware is required beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout board and display. The documentation is minimal and the design appears to be a simple logic demonstration or class exercise.

This design implements a finite state machine that counts from 0 to 3, with the count advanced by a button press when the first input is enabled. The count is displayed on a seven-segment display, and other inputs provide additional logic for experimentation. It is a copy of the author's earlier Tiny Tapeout submission and is intended for use on a Steam Deck. Testing requires enabling the first input, turning off all others, and pressing the button to progress the FSM.

This design is a four-bit adder that takes two four-bit binary numbers and produces their sum on a seven-segment display, with the carry shown on the decimal point. It uses four full adders feeding a binary-to-seven-segment decoder, and is tested by setting the two numbers on DIP switches. Display of sums greater than nine is noted as questionable, and no external hardware is needed. The project is a straightforward arithmetic and display demonstration.

This design is a 4-word by 4-bit read/write RAM with separate data and address inputs and a write enable signal. Data is written to the addressed location when write enable is asserted, and the stored word is presented on the read data outputs. It is tested by setting the data and address lines, cycling write enable, and then reading the value on the read data outputs. No external hardware is required, and the design serves as a basic memory block.

This design implements a small R-2R digital-to-analog converter by adding a resistor ladder to the outputs of D flip-flops. It is tested by attaching an external R-2R ladder and a non-inverting op-amp to the output to observe the analog voltage. The design requires external resistors and an op-amp, and the documentation notes that an AND gate was removed and a pin is used as a passthrough. The project is a simple mixed-signal experiment.

This design implements the Chi function of the Xoodoo permutation protected with threshold implementation using two shares. It is tested by setting the last four inputs, and the outputs are connected to a seven-segment display. The design is a cryptographic building block aimed at side-channel resistance, and no external hardware is mentioned. The documentation is very brief and does not provide detailed test procedures or expected results.

This design implements the Chi function of the Xoodoo permutation protected with threshold implementation using three shares. It is tested by setting all inputs, and the outputs drive a seven-segment display. The design is a cryptographic building block intended for side-channel resistance, and no external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal and lacks detailed test instructions or expected behavior.

This design displays a BCD counter on a seven-segment display, with the segment logic simplified using sum-of-products equations. It can run automatically with the clock switch on and all toggle switches in zero position, or individual BCD bits can be toggled with the clock off. The design includes a decimal point toggle and is intended for educational or demonstration purposes. No external hardware is required beyond the standard board and display.

This design implements a finite state machine that cycles through the letters A, d, and i on a seven-segment display when a button is pushed. It is tested by connecting a push button and a seven-segment display, then pressing the button to advance the sequence. The design is a simple test FSM, likely for educational purposes, and requires only minimal external hardware. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand its operation.
